Bat Behavior at Commercial Wind Turbines as Revealed by 3-D Thermal Videography Thesis Directed by Assistant Professor Aaron J. Corcoran.

## **ABSTRACT**

The wind industry is rapidly growing, yet lethal interactions between bats and industrial-scale wind turbines remain an ecological drawback of this valuable renewable energy source. Previous research has utilized two-dimensional video to describe bat

behavior, however it is unable to provide quantifiable spatial metrics that may be important in determining why collisions occur and inform development of collision minimization systems. Our study represents the first utility-scale application of threedimensional video, a method capable of accurately measuring the position of animals in space, used to measure bat activity patterns at commercial wind turbines. We reconstructed 22,479 flight paths of nocturnal aerial animals across 89 recording nights at two wind turbines in a utility-scale wind energy facility in Iowa, USA between August and October of 2021. We observed 68% of vertebrate animal flights at heights within the rotor-swept zone where they are at danger of colliding with blades. Activity was 300% higher in the lower half of the rotor-swept zone (below the turbine nacelle) compared to the upper half. We found that activity within and above the rotor swept area is concentrated during a small range of dates in late August, early evening hours, and for winds blowing to the south between 3 and 6 meters per second, supporting the theory that bat mortality is related to peaks in migration activity. For a subset of 23 nights distributed across the sampling period, we manually classified the behavior of 4,252 flight paths. Linear flight behaviors were more common above the turbine, whereas non-linear behaviors were more common at altitudes in the lower rotor-swept zone. We also

reconstructed two collisions with the turbine which suggests that wind turbulence may be

a proximate cause of collision. Our findings indicate that while three-dimensional video may not be necessary for general activity studies, it will be valuable in understanding how best to deploy targeted minimization systems, such as acoustic deterrents, and

provide in-depth characterizations of bat behavior near turbines that will help elucidate the underlying cause of collisions.

## **CHAPTER I**

## **INTRODUCTION**

Energy crises in the late 20[th] century, namely the oil embargo of 1973, highlighted a global need to diversify energy resources beyond fossil fuels (Mittlefehldt, 2018).

Countries recognized renewable energy sources as reliable alternatives and more recently as viable options to mitigate climate change (Luderer et al., 2014). Consequently,

renewable energy industries, such as solar, wind, and biofuel, grew rapidly over the last several decades and renewable energy production now accounts for about one quarter of global power generation (IRENA, 2022; REN21, 2022). Wind is favored as a renewable energy source because it is possible to generate electricity using wind turbines in most countries, turbines do not emit greenhouse gas during electricity production, and energy production costs are competitive with other renewables like solar (Jaber, 2014; REN21, 2022). Globally, nearly $1.3 trillion USD was spent to develop wind energy over the last decade, and wind energy production has increased exponentially since 2000 in regions like Europe, North America, and Asia (IRENA & CPI, 2023; Kaldellis & Zafirakis, 2011). Currently, China, the United States, and Germany are the leading wind energy producers, however, the industry is expected to grow globally as other countries, such as Brazil and India, are making large investments towards developing wind energy facilities (REN21, 2022).

While wind energy is economically beneficial to global energy generation and contributes to countering climate change, there is evidence that wind turbines negatively affect wildlife, especially flying animals that collide with turbines. Video surveys have

recorded birds (Aschwanden et al., 2015; McClure et al., 2021) and bats (Cryan et al. 2014; Horn et al., 2008) flying near turbine structural components and carcasses collected below wind turbines exhibit injuries (e.g. lacerations, fractures, limb amputations)

consistent with contacting turbines during flight (Baerwald et al., 2008; Ferri et al.,

2011). Animals can collide with stationary turbine structures, such as the monopole, but collisions primarily occur in the rotor swept zone (RSZ; Figure 1) where the rotor blades strike an animal in flight (Choi et al., 2020). Research focused on addressing bird

fatalities has resulted in simple interventions that could reduce fatalities and do not affect energy production, such as aviation lighting (Gehring et al., 2009). However, reducing bat fatalities has been a challenge despite considerable effort. There is no consensus as to why bats are attracted to wind turbines (Guest et al., 2022) and the only proven mitigation method, curtailment (turning turbines off at low wind speeds when they produce relatively little energy), reduces energy production. Figure 1. The anatomy of a large wind turbine (art by Maddison Simmons and Gail Shultz).

Australian wildlife surveys recorded the first evidence of bat fatalities caused by turbine collisions (Hall and Richards, 1972; Tate, 1952). Since then, bat turbine fatalities are recognized as a global issue with carcasses observed at wind facilities across North America (Davy et al., 2020; Erickson and Gritski, 2003; Kerns and Kerlinger, 2004; Brown and Hamilton, 2006a; Jain et al., 2011), South America (Barros et al., 2015; Escobar et al., 2015), Europe (Camina, 2012; Georgiakakis et al., 2012; Lehnert et al. 2014; Măntoiu et al., 2020; Marques et al., 2018), Africa (Doty and Martin, 2013) and Asia (Chou et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2013). In well-studied regions, such as North America and Europe, it is currently estimated that hundreds of thousands of bats die each year from colliding with turbines, with millions likely dying over the last two decades (Voigt et al., 2022). Furthermore, the rapid expansion of wind energy with newer technology, such as taller turbines and larger rotor swept zones (Wiser et al., 2022), that pose greater risk to bats (Barclay et al., 2007) suggest the problem is only expected to worsen. Wind energy development can cause large bat population declines, sometimes as much as 91%, during a short period of only a few years (Davy et al., 2021). Across a longer range, effects can become dire with certain species risking extinction in the next 50 to 100 years (Frick et al., 2017; Friedenberg and Frick., 2021). Loss of these species could have far-reaching environmental and economic effects. For example, species affected by turbines perform valuable environmental services, such as pest control (Fill et al., 2022), likely worth billions of dollars to agricultural industries (Boyles et al., 2011; Maine and Boyles, 2015). Therefore, it is important to address turbine fatalities to prevent bat population decline and global economic and environmental losses.

Technological solutions such as acoustic deterrents and turbine curtailment algorithms have been proposed as methods to prevent bat turbine fatalities. Bats use ultrasonic echolocation frequencies for spatial orientation, communication, and foraging (Jones and Holderied, 2007). However, some bats avoid ultrasound from external

sources, such as conspecifics (Loeb and Britzke, 2010) and insects (Hristov and Conner, 2005). Acoustic deterrents are devices that broadcast high frequency sounds used by bats and are an active research area to prevent bat fatalities. Deterrents mounted to turbine nacelles can reduce bat fatalities by 21-78%, however deterrent effectiveness varies by species (Arnett et al., 2013; Weaver et al., 2020) and possible increase fatality rates of others (Schirmacher, 2020). Because higher frequencies attenuate more quickly in the air, it is difficult if not impossible to design acoustic deterrents that cover the entire rotorswept area of large turbines at all frequencies used by bats (Arnett et al., 2013). An alternative to acoustic deterrents is curtailment, where rotors are automatically feathered or slowed during conditions associated with high collision risk (e.g., low wind speed). Curtailment is currently the most effective method to reduce bat fatalities (Adams et al., 2021; Whitby et al., 2021; Voigt et al., 2022) and in some instances, turbine curtailment can reduce fatality rates by 33-79% (Whitby et al., 2021). Although energy losses can seem minimal, ranging from 0.6 to 3.2% loss in annual energy production (Whitby et al., 2021), it is important for these systems to be highly optimized to prevent any unnecessary energy production losses accrued during curtailment (Rogers, 2020). Turbine curtailment models are typically developed to find the conditions associated with the highest fatality rates or activity levels at wind turbines (Behr et al., 2017; Barré et al., 2023; Korner-Nievergelt et al., 2013). For fatality prevention systems to be effective, it is

necessary to understand what bat species, flight behaviors, and environmental conditions

are associated with high collision risk.

Bat turbine fatalities vary regionally; however, fatality rates are strongly

associated with species with certain flight patterns and evolutionary strategies. Globally, aerial-hawking bats, or those that capture prey in the open air (Jones and Rydell, 2003), that travel at high altitudes tend to collide with turbines more frequently than other bat species. For example, Davy’s naked-backed bat ( _Pteronotus davyi_ ) in Mexico, common noctules ( _Nyctalus noctule_ ) in Europe, and Hoary bats ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ) in the United States and Canada (Arnett et al., 2016). However, this trend does not encompass the full scope of species at risk. For instance, a study in Puerto Rico recorded several fatalities among frugivorous phyllostomid bats which tend to fly at low altitudes, like _Artibeus jamaicensis_ (Rodríguez-Durán and Feliciano-Robles, 2015). It is important to highlight that little is known about fatality trends in tropical regions with diverse bat species, like Asia, South America, and Africa (Arnett et al., 2016). This is likely because many countries from these regions have only begun investing heavily in wind energy during the last decade (IRENA, 2022). In temperate areas like Europe and North America, where bat turbine fatalities have been studied more extensively since the late 2000s, fatalities tend to follow global trends with high-flying, aerial-hawking species composing most

fatalities (Arnett et al., 2016). However, these species are also predominantly tree-

roosting migrants (Arnett et al., 2016; EUROBAT, 2023). Migratory bats are

characterized by seasonal movement over long distances, sometimes over 1500km, and several degrees in latitude (Flemming and Eby, 2003). As opposed to more permanent roosting sites in enclosed spaces such as caves, tree bats exhibit ephemeral roosting

behavior and rest in semi-protected sites found in tree cavities or foliage (Kunz and Lumsden, 2003). In Europe, tree-roosting, migratory species, specifically common pipistrelles ( _Pipistrellus pipistrellus_ , 22%), Nathusius’ pipistrelles ( _Pipistrellus nathusii_ , 16%), and common noctules ( _Nyctalus noctule_ , 15%; EUROBAT, 2023) compose about half of all bat turbine fatalities. In North America, the vast majority (78.4%) of recovered carcasses are tree-roosting migratory bats. These species include hoary bats ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ , 38%), eastern red bats ( _Lasiurus borealis_ , 22%), and silver-haired bats

( _Lasionyvteris noctivagans_ , 18.4%; Arnett and Baerwald, 2013). Because fatality rates are especially high for migratory tree bats in the United States, several hypotheses have been proposed to explain why turbine collisions are common among these species (Table 1). However, these hypotheses are not mutually exclusive and may be acting synergistically at varying spatial scales. Collisions could be random if all bats exhibit equal collision risk, however this seems unlikely because risk is biased by age, sex, and species. Juveniles of some species may be at higher risk as they have less flight experience. Population analysis by Kruszynski et al. (2022) concluded that juvenile Nathusius’ pipistrelles are disproportionately killed by wind turbines near forests and bodies of water. Additionally, collision risk is likely related to an individual’s sex, for example female common noctules spend more time near turbines and approach turbines more often than males (Roeleke et al. 2016). Sex-biased risk may also be

species-specific because hoary bat, eastern red bat, and silver-haired bat fatalities are mostly male (Arnett et al. 2008). Lastly, tree bat collisions in North America occur

mostly during the fall migration between August and September, and migratory species constitute the majority of fatalities during this period (Arnett and Baerwald, 2013; Choi et

al., 2020; Fiedler et al., 2007). In contrast, summer-resident species, such as little brown bats ( _Myotis lucifugus_ ) and big brown bats ( _Eptesicus fuscus_ ), maintain regular activity, but constitute only 0-13.5% of turbine fatalities (Arnett et al., 2008). This suggests that other seasonally migratory species are at greater turbine collision risk.

Because turbine fatalities occur mostly in the fall, it is also possible that turbine collisions occur because of migratory behaviors. In the United States, most wind energy facilities are in Texas, Iowa, and Oklahoma (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2023; Figure 2). These regions are in modelled migratory routes taken by eastern red bats, hoary bats, and silver-haired bats (Wieringa et al., 2021; Figure 3). Therefore, bats may be coincidentally colliding with turbines because wind energy facilities were constructed along their migration routes. Some bat species may also be at increased risk for coincidental collisions because they are naturally active in air space that overlaps with the RSZ. For example, European free-tailed bats ( _Tadarida teniotis_ ) are more likely to fly at heights within a turbine RSZ compared to _Myotis_ sp. which are rarely detected far from the ground (Wellig et al. 2018). Roemer et al. (2020) reconfirmed that flight altitude is correlated to collision risk and high-flying _Tadarida_ species are at higher collision risk than low-flying _Myotis_ species.
